title: What to hand a developer with a design
excerpt: Hand a developer the type, colors, spacing, components, and states, including empty and error. A flat picture of the happy path forces them to invent the rest of the product.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out, a handoff someone else can search without guessing what is inside.
caption: Titles facing out of the crates. Hand over the parts, not a closed cover. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a design handoff include?
faqs.answer: Type sizes, colors by role, a small spacing scale, named components, and the states those components can be in. Include the real words, the redirects, and the image crops. A screenshot of the happy path is not a spec.

faqs.question: Which states are usually missing?
faqs.answer: Empty, error, loading, focus, and disabled. Hover does not replace focus. A blank area is not an empty state, and an error that says invalid input does not tell anyone how to fix the field.

faqs.question: How should you review the first built page?
faqs.answer: Open it on a real URL and compare it to the decisions, not to a screenshot at a different pixel ratio. Tab through it, submit a bad form, and turn on reduced motion. If page two is built from new one-off styles, the handoff or the build has drifted.

markdown:
Hand a developer the type, the colors, the spacing, the components, and the states. Include the words. Include what the page does when it fails. Design handoff for developers is that package, shared in a place both people can open, before anyone is asked to "just build the picture."

A flat export of the happy path is a poster. The engineer will invent the rest, and you will then review their inventions as if they were mistakes. Give them the decisions instead.

## Type, color, and space, as decisions

Name the typefaces, the sizes you actually use, the weights, and the line heights. A screenshot is not a spec. Two people measuring the same heading with a ruler will not match. Write the scale down: a display size, a title, a body, a label. Say what is allowed to wrap and what should stay one line.

Name the colors by role. Background, text, muted text, line, primary action, danger. Hex values belong next to the roles. "The blue from the brand deck" is not a role. If a campaign may add one accent, say so, and say where it may not appear. Buttons should stay on the system color.

Name the spacing. A small set of steps beats a unique margin on every frame. Four or eight steps is enough for a small site. The developer should be able to map those steps into the layout system, whether that is Tailwind or something else, without guessing which 13-pixel gap was intentional.

Say the maximum line length for body text, and the page width. These two numbers prevent a beautiful desktop frame from becoming a full-bleed paragraph on a wide monitor. They are design decisions. Leaving them implicit is how the built site feels looser than the file.

Hanabi records this in Figma, in variables or a simple style board, and builds it in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind. The tool is less important than the fact that the values exist outside a flattened PNG. Illustrator files for marks should be included as the real vectors, not as a screenshot of the logo.

## Components, named by the job

Hand over the components you expect to reuse. Button, text field, select, checkbox, navigation, footer, card, price row, dialog. Name them by the job. A later visual change should not force a rename, and the engineer should not have to invent "blue card" because the file had no name.

For each component, show the parts: label, icon if any, helper text, and the action. Show the sizes you truly need. One button size is often enough. Three sizes, delivered without a rule, will be used at random.

Show the component in a dull context, not only in the hero. A button on a white page, a button on a photograph, a button next to a secondary action. If you have not decided the secondary action, decide it. "Text link beside the primary button" is a decision. Silence will be interpreted differently by every person who touches the page.

Include the focus and disabled presentations. The WCAG overview describes four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A handoff that includes only the resting state fails the operable principle the moment someone tabs. You do not need to attach the entire standard. You need a visible focus style and labels that are real text, not placeholders standing in for labels.

If the component has an accessible name that differs from the visible words, write both. Icon-only buttons are the usual miss. "Close" and "Search" must exist as words somewhere. A picture of an X is not a handoff.

## States are the rest of the design

For every interactive thing, provide the states that can happen. Default, hover if you mean it, focus, active, disabled, error, success, loading, empty. Hover is not a substitute for focus. Loading is not a spinner dropped in a corner with no sentence.

Write what the empty state says and what it offers. An empty library can point at the action that fills it. An empty search can suggest a narrower try. A blank area is not an empty state. It is a missing one.

Write the error in the product's voice. "Enter a work email" is a decision. "Invalid input" is an abdication. Put the message next to the field it refers to, in the file, so the build does not attach it to the top of the page by default.

Write the loading rule. What stays still. What is allowed to shift. web.dev's description of cumulative layout shift is the practical reason: a good experience keeps shift at 0.1 or less. If your skeleton screen is a different shape from the loaded content, you designed a jump. Show both shapes matching, or accept the shift on purpose and say so.

Cover the awkward content. The longest product name you expect. The shortest. A user with no avatar. A price with no discount and a price with one. These are not polish. They are the cases that break a tight card.

Mobile is a state of the layout, not a second file you might get to. If the navigation becomes a dialog, draw the dialog, including how it closes. If the table becomes a list, draw the list. A note that says "make it responsive" is the poster problem again.

## Words, links, and the edges of the page

Put the real copy in the frames, or in a document keyed to the frames. Headings, buttons, errors, empty states, and the title element for each template. A developer should not write the offer at 7 p.m. because the text boxes said "Headline goes here."

Specify the links. What opens in the same tab. What is an external site. What happens to a retired URL. Redirects are part of the design of a redesign. If you do not list them, the old campaign will outrank the new page, and that will be treated as an engineering surprise.

Specify images. The crop, the focal point, and the alt text when the image means something. Decorative images can be marked as such. A hero with no alt decision will get the filename as its description. Hand over assets at the size you intend to ship, or hand over a rule for how they are cropped in code. A 6000-pixel export and a prayer is how pages miss their loading target. Largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, as web.dev states it, is hard to hit with an accidental mural.

Include the email or the confirmation the form produces, if that message is part of the experience. Many handoffs stop at the button. The user continues into an inbox. Design that sentence too.

Mark what is a template and what is a one-off. A case study template with slots is a gift. Six unique art-directed case studies are a different scope. Say which one you drew.

## How to hand it over without a novel

Use one source of truth. A Figma file with a page called Foundations and a page called Components will do. A prototype in Framer helps when sequence is the question, and it should not contradict the file. If they diverge, name the winner before the build starts.

Walk through it once, on a call, with the person who will build. Thirty minutes on the states is worth more than a 40-page PDF nobody opens. Record the decisions that changed on the call inside the file. A Hanabi project keeps those notes where the client can find them later, in the portal with the other docs and brand files.

Invite questions that sound pedantic. "What if the name wraps?" "What if there is no image?" Those questions are the handoff working. A silent engineer is often an engineer who has decided to guess.

Do not hand over fifty explorations. Hand over the chosen direction and, if useful, one rejected direction with a sentence about why. The rejected direction prevents a well-meaning rebuild of the idea you already killed.

Say what is intentionally unfinished. If illustration is coming later, mark the slot and the fallback color. If a page is out of scope, do not leave a half-drawn frame that looks like a promise. The out list from the scope belongs at the front of the handoff.

## What you should get back

Ask for a first built page early, on a real URL, with real type. Compare it to the decisions, not to a screenshot at a different pixel ratio. Space, type, and the primary action should be obvious. The rest of the pages should reuse the components. If page two is built from new one-off styles, the handoff or the build has drifted. Find out which, while the fix is still cheap.

Review states in the browser. Tab, submit a bad form, throttle the network, and turn on reduced motion. This is the QA pass. It is also the proof that the handoff was complete enough to build.

The names you chose will be said in every review after this. If they are job names, the team will still understand them when the color changes. The piece on [component names a small team can say](/blog/component-names-a-small-team-can-say) is the next read if the file is full of "final-v3-card-blue" and nobody can say it in a sentence.

If you want a second set of eyes on a handoff before it becomes code, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the file and the out list. The useful outcome is a package an engineer can build without inventing the empty state.
